Title: Passage 1: New Light From Green Corn
Author: by Gloria W. Lannom and Jason Baird Jackson
Content: `text(Each year)`, many American Indian communities gather together to celebrate and give thanks for the gifts of nature. The most important gift is corn. To give thanks for `text(each year's)` corn crop, Green Corn Ceremonies have been held for many `text(hundreds of years)`.
While not all native peoples observe this celebration, it `text(once)` was widespread. Today's Green Corn Ceremonies are held among the Yuchi, Creek, Seminole, Shawnee, and Cherokee peoples.

According to Seminole legend, the Corn Mother, goddess of farming, created corn by rubbing her body and causing kernels of corn to appear. Wherever the kernels were planted, cornstalks quickly sprang up.

The Green Corn Ceremony is a celebration of cleansing, renewal, and thanksgiving. It is held when the moon is full in `text(late June)` or `text(early July)` and when the ears of new corn are ripe and ready for roasting. According to tradition, tribe members clean and repair their chickee¹ camps near the dance grounds to prepare for the `text(four-day)` celebration. They settle arguments. They may make new clothes.

During the ceremony, many stomp dances are performed. A stomp dance is a weaving line of dancers in `text(single)` file. Some stomp dances are social dances, such as the Catfish Dance and the Fire Ant Dance. Other dances, such as the Feather Dance, are sacred. The em-ma-pah-thi (the “bundle carrier,” a tribal medicine man) chants songs and the men sing back to him. The women, dressed in their finest clothing, keep the rhythm for the stomp dancers by shaking rattles tied to their legs. These noisemakers used to be made of turtle shells, but today they are more likely to be empty tin cans. On the `text(last day)` of the celebration, the women put out their cooking fires. Long ago, this was the only time of the `text(year)` when no fires burned. Ears of corn are placed on new firewood on the main fire pit. With prayers and special words, the em-ma-pah-thi takes tools from his sacred medicine bundle and lights the new fire. All the other fires are relighted from this `text(one)` fire.

The men, who have had nothing to eat for a `text(day and a half)`, eat roasted fresh corn that the women have picked. Traditionally, this was the `text(first)` fresh corn (not dried) that they ate since the previous `text(year's)` harvest. Today, everyone feasts on many delicious things. The end of the Green Corn Ceremony marks the start of the new `text(year)`.
